title: Jank-Free Animations
description: Learn how to build animations that maintain 60fps by respecting the frame budget, avoiding main-thread work, and choosing the right animation APIs.

data.text: Jank is the perception of stutter or dropped frames during animation or scrolling. At 60Hz displays the browser must render a frame every 16.67 ms. If JavaScript, layout, paint, or composite take longer than that, frames are dropped and the user notices.

Every frame has a strict time budget. Understanding where that time goes helps you identify which work to remove or move off the main thread. Long tasks, layout thrashing, and heavy paint are the biggest frame budget killers.

data.title: Frame Budget Breakdown
data.code:
Frame Budget at 60Hz (16.67 ms per frame):

JavaScript (app logic + rAF callbacks):   ~4 ms
Style recalculation:                        ~1 ms
Layout (if triggered):                     ~3-8 ms
Paint (if triggered):                      ~2-6 ms
Composite (always):                        ~1 ms

If JavaScript alone exceeds ~10 ms, the frame is missed.
Common jank causes:
- Long tasks (>50 ms)
- Layout thrashing inside rAF
- Expensive paint (large shadows, blur)
- Synchronous XHR or heavy event handlers
- Garbage collection during animation

data.text: CSS transitions and keyframe animations are the cheapest way to animate because browsers can run them on the compositor thread. As long as you animate only transform and opacity, the main thread is free for JavaScript work.

data.title: Performant CSS Transitions
data.content: Use CSS transitions for smooth, GPU-friendly state changes.

data.text: For complex, interactive, or state-driven animations, use requestAnimationFrame. It synchronizes your callback with the browser's paint cycle, so you never write a DOM change that the browser cannot use.

data.title: Smooth rAF Animation
data.content: Build a custom animation loop with requestAnimationFrame.

data.text: When animating in response to user input — dragging, scrolling, swiping — keep the animation loop as thin as possible. Read input values, compute the next frame, and write only transform or opacity.

data.title: Drag Gesture with rAF
data.content: Keep drag animations inside the frame budget.

data.text: Framer Motion, React Spring, and Motion One all default to transform and opacity, use rAF internally, and batch work to stay inside the frame budget. Prefer them over manual style manipulation for declarative animations.

data.title: Framer Motion List Animation
data.content: Animate list items with layout animations.

data.text: Some users prefer reduced motion due to vestibular disorders or personal preference. Use the prefers-reduced-motion media query to detect this and disable or simplify animations.

data.title: Reduced Motion Support
Animation Jank in Production
data.text: Animation performance varies across devices. A smooth 60fps animation on a desktop may jank on a mid-range phone. Always test on real low-end hardware and use Chrome DevTools CPU throttling to simulate slower devices during development.

terms.definition: The time available to render one frame; 16.67 ms at 60Hz.
Browser API that schedules callbacks before the next paint, aligning JavaScript with the rendering cycle.
A media query that indicates whether the user has requested fewer or no animations.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: 60fps requires each frame to finish within 16.67 ms
Animating transform and opacity is compositor-only and safe for 60fps
Animating layout properties forces layout + paint every frame
requestAnimationFrame synchronizes JavaScript with the paint cycle
Keep rAF callbacks small: read input, compute, write transform
Test animations on real low-end devices and with CPU throttling
data.takeaway: Jank-free animations are built by choosing the right properties, batching DOM work, and always staying within the frame budget. Compositor-only properties and requestAnimationFrame are your primary tools.
